sections.html:
Boston is the state capital and the seat of Suffolk County. The 2020 census counted 675,647 residents, the most of any city in Massachusetts. A good share of the land came from fill, and Back Bay is one of the areas built on gravel hauled in by train, so soil, basements and foundations differ a lot from one block to the next.

The city recognizes 23 neighborhoods, including Allston, Back Bay, Beacon Hill, Charlestown, Dorchester, East Boston, Fenway, Hyde Park, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, Roslindale, Roxbury, South Boston, the South End and West Roxbury. Each can have a different mix of triple-deckers, rowhouses, condos and single families, and all are billed through the same city tax system.

Winters are cold and stormy, so roofs, gutters, heating systems and pipes take the most wear. The median home was built in 1947, which means many houses are due for roof, wiring or boiler work. Waterfront and low-lying streets deserve a closer look at basement moisture. If the repairs are more than you want to take on, selling as-is is one way out, since a cash buyer prices the condition in and you skip the contractor visits.

sections.h2: Who bills and collects Boston property tax
sections.html:
Two offices share the work: Assessing sets the value and Tax Collection sends and collects the bill. Both sit in City Hall at 1 City Hall Square. Assessing is in Room 301, and the Collector is at Window M-30.

Boston runs on a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year and bills quarterly. The first and second quarter bills are estimates built from last year's value and rate. The real rate shows up on the third quarter bill, typically issued in late December.

The 2026 rate is $12.40 per $1,000 for residential property and $26.96 for commercial, industrial and personal property, because Boston classifies property and charges the two classes different rates. Proposition 2½, passed by voters in 1980, caps how fast the city's total levy can grow, but it does not limit growth in an individual assessment.

The residential exemption takes part of a home's value out of taxation if you own it and live in it as your primary residence. It saved qualified homeowners up to $4,353.74 last fiscal year, and the credit is applied to the third quarter bill in late December.

For FY2027 the application is due by April 1, 2027. A recent home rule petition widened the rules: owners who recorded a deed at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds and moved in between January 1 and June 30, 2026 may now qualify for the current year. Owners who owned and occupied on January 1, 2026 still qualify.

  • You can claim the exemption on one property only.
  • Filing does not postpone a payment that is due.
  • Other exemptions can stack with it, but taxable value cannot drop below 10 percent of assessed value, with exceptions for some residents with physical ailments or financial hardship.
  • Applications are downloaded from the Boston Property Lookup tool after the December bills go out.

A buyer who moves in can apply for the exemption, so do not promise a buyer a tax figure. Send them to the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center to see what the current bill looks like.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my Boston assessment?
sections.html:
File an abatement application with the Assessing Department by mail or in person before February 1, 2027 for FY2027. Assessing's direct line is 617-635-4288. If the department denies the request, you have three months from its decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board at 100 Cambridge Street, 2nd Floor, Suite 200, Boston, MA 02114, phone 617-727-3100.

Ask the Collector how an open abatement affects the bill you currently owe.

If you own a condo with a deeded parking space, check for two bills. A condo unit appears as class CD and the parking space as class CP, and both must be paid because together they equal the full property value.

sections.h2: What does selling a Boston house involve?
sections.html:
In Massachusetts a house sale is a recorded transaction, and a real estate attorney is normally part of it. Attorneys handle buying and selling by law and by practice, and the deed to 80 to 90 percent of properties is filed as recorded land at the county Registry of Deeds. For Boston that means the Suffolk County registry.

Three state rules show up for most sellers:

  • Deeds excise. The deeds tax is $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed.
  • Smoke and CO certificate. A seller needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the alarms meet requirements for a sale. The fire department charges a fee.
  • Inspection waivers. State regulation 760 CMR 74 says sellers of certain residential properties will not condition an offer on a waiver of the home inspection.

A cash sale keeps all three in place. What changes is who is waiting on repairs and financing.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html:
Boston sellers lose time when the paperwork shows up late, so collect it first.

  • Your latest quarterly tax bill and proof of payment for each quarter so far.
  • Any abatement application or Appellate Tax Board filing, with the decision letter if you have one.
  • For a condo, both the unit bill (class CD) and the parking space bill (class CP).
  • Proof of the residential exemption you have been receiving, so your attorney can explain to the buyer that it will not carry over.
  • Your deed and mortgage payoff information, since the deed goes to the Suffolk County registry at closing.

Call the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center at 617-635-4287 with questions about the current year. Because the first two quarterly bills are estimates and the true rate arrives with the third, the amount that has to be split between you and the buyer can shift late in the year, so ask your attorney how the closing statement will handle it.

Unpaid tax can be settled from the sale proceeds at closing, which lowers what you take home. Get the exact amount owed from the city before you sign. For current-year questions call 617-635-4287, and for earlier years call the Collector at 617-635-4131.

If the property came to you through probate, tax questions can run alongside other deadlines. Our pages on the Massachusetts estate tax, capital gains and homestead protection cover those separately.

A workable order is to request the payoff, confirm any open abatement with the Collector, line up the fire department certificate, then give your attorney the figures so the closing statement is right the first time.

faqs.q: What is the Boston residential property tax rate?
faqs.a: The 2026 residential rate is $12.40 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial, industrial and personal property rate is $26.96 per $1,000. The final rate for a fiscal year appears on the third quarter bill.

faqs.q: When are Boston property tax abatement applications due?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2027, the deadline is February 1, 2027. You file with the Assessing Department by mail or in person. If it is denied, you have three months from the decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

faqs.q: Can I get Boston's residential exemption if I just bought my home?
faqs.a: Possibly. Owners who recorded a deed at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds and occupied the home between January 1 and June 30, 2026 may qualify for FY2027. The application is due April 1, 2027.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay tax on a condo parking space in Boston?
faqs.a: Yes, if you receive a separate bill. The unit is class CD and the parking space is class CP, and both bills must be paid because together they make up the full property value.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Boston house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, in general. The unpaid amount can be settled from the proceeds at closing. Call the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center at 617-635-4287 for the exact amount owed.
